How can we use AI to digitize spare parts management?

Recent advances in AI have taken the technology from a simple talking point to an essential tool across all industries. For many companies looking to optimize traditional and legacy problems, even modest productivity gains from AI could provide a market advantage.. However, some industries continue to lag behind, especially when it comes to managing their spare parts.

The hesitation might be due, in part, to the fact that spare parts workflows are built on complex supply chains and operations, as well as highly traditional processes, which make it difficult to integrate AI.

Spare parts management is inherently risky. Because of this, many companies are wary of the potential disruption to their operations that could happen from adopting what may be a fleeting trend. This reluctance has been evident over the past decade, as Industry 4.0 has grown in importance. Valtech's research supports this, showing that
the manufacturing
industry is cautious about adopting new technologies
, fearing disrupting — and potentially compromising — established ways of doing things. In this study, they also say,

“Unlike digital-native or SaaS companies where many best practices in digital transformation have come from, traditional B2B manufacturers face a unique legacy and operational focus. Their revenue depends on physical products, with extensive operations involving production,
supply chains and warehouses. This influences the organizational structure, talent pool, cultures, and well-established processes.”
Where AI can make a real difference: Getting past the "hype"

However, it would be a mistake to compare recent advancements in AI with the "hyped" innovations of the past decade. Many of these pre-AI innovations failed to gain traction because they seemed to promise to solve all parts availability problems, but were overly complex and required significant IT support to be used effectively. One example of this has been additive manufacturing, which initially seemed to offer a solution to the spare parts problem but is actually quite difficult to scale due to post-processing requirements like sanding or the inability to scale production quickly.

Recently, AI has been on the opposite side of this spectrum. The technology has been widely adopted in almost every industry and profession by simplifying complex processes for non-experts. We could already see this happening in
late 2022 when ChatGPT was first released

. People could start using it immediately without having to watch instructional videos. While there are some nuances to using ChatGPT, for most people, it performs tasks as requested without requiring complicated prompt engineering.

Thanks to recent advancements with ChatGPT, AI has gone from a buzzword to opening the doors to other machine learning applications. AI can make a real difference for other Industry 4.0 technologies by simplifying their use. For example, spare parts inventory management software was oftentimes previously too complicated, had low adoption rates, and caused inaccuracies in spare parts inventory. Users were more likely to complete spare parts management tasks if the tools had AI features that made completing steps
simpler and faster by utilizing better data extraction.
Innovation has historically been trapped in R&D departments

If we look back to the pre-2020 era, AI was confined to early adopters and technically savvy experts. Back then, the adoption of digital technologies was primarily limited to research and development (R&D) departments, where infrastructure, budgets, and processes were available for experimentation with innovation.

This cautious approach also limited the potential for new ideas to significantly benefit the business, particularly when it came to solving persistent problems such as spare parts management. By confining digital innovation to the R&D department as a testing ground, companies inadvertently prevented these technologies from driving widespread change and innovation throughout the organization.

In this article, we look at how companies can start effectively digitizing their spare parts management, what they should look out for in the process, and where AI can add the most value to their operations.
Change your mind — for every challenge ask yourself whether AI can help

With a number of emerging technologies now available, it's worth evaluating your current spare parts management processes to identify areas that could benefit from digitization through AI. By focusing on processes that are known to be challenging or error-prone, you can also make it much easier for your team and company to adopt the new technology as well.

For example, when you set a clear goal, you might decide toreduce duplicate part entries from 15% to 0%.This targeted approach not only clarifies the goals for digitizing the process but also provides a measurable metric for evaluating success and gives you a general sense of direction when you start looking for solutions.
An overview of where AI can help in digitization

Not sure which aspect of AI to prioritize? Start with AI's inherent strengths: data cleaning, analysis, and predictive forecasting. This set of capabilities fits seamlessly into spare parts management. Every piece of information associated with a part can be digitized and leveraged effectively through AI-driven tools to fix most spare parts management challenges today.
Data capture

At the heart of successful spare parts management is efficient data collection. AI can significantly improve this process by automating the extraction of data from various sources, such as invoices, purchase orders, and maintenance records. Through the use of optical character recognition (OCR) technology, AI algorithms can quickly scan and digitize data from unstructured formats, significantly reducing the time and effort required for manual data entry. In addition, AI-powered data capture systems can intelligently validate and cross-reference information to maintain the accuracy and completeness of spare parts inventory databases.
Advanced AI can also improve
data collection and extract valuable insights from
unstructured data sources

such as maintenance records, sensor readouts, and service reports. By analyzing diverse data sets, AI can identify patterns, trends, and correlations that human operators might miss. This enables proactive maintenance strategies and optimized parts procurement. This holistic approach to data collection enables organizations to make data-driven decisions, improve asset reliability, and minimize downtime, ultimately increasing operational efficiency and reducing costs.
Data cleaning

Data cleaning, especially given the vast amount of data generated by modern industrial systems, is a critical yet time-consuming task in spare parts management. To automate and streamline this process and ensure data integrity and reliability, AI offers a game-changing solution. Using machine learning algorithms, AI systems can detect and correct errors, inconsistencies, and anomalies in spare parts data, improving its quality and usability. In addition, AI-driven data cleaning tools can adapt and self-improve over time. They learn from past corrections to continually improve their accuracy and effectiveness (including using external datasets to enrich uncleaned data sets).

In addition to error detection and correction, AI-driven data cleaning can also enrich spare parts data by standardizing formats, resolving duplicates, and filling in missing information. Using natural language processing (NLP) techniques, AI systems can extract valuable metadata from unstructured text fields, such as part descriptions and specifications. This further enhances the detail and richness of parts data.
Big data-based prediction modeling

In the era of big data, companies have access to large amounts of historical and real-time data that can be used for predictive modeling in spare parts management. AI techniques, such as machine and deep learning, make it possible to develop complex predictive models
to anticipate equipment failures, fluctuating demand, and supply chain disruptions. By analyzing historical usage patterns, maintenance records, and environmental factors,
predictive models can forecast spare parts demand
with remarkable accuracy. This enables proactive inventory management and resource allocation.

AI algorithms can also continuously learn and adapt to evolving data patterns, improving predictive accuracy and reliability over time. By integrating real-time sensor data and Internet of Things (IoT) devices into predictive models, organizations can implement proactive maintenance strategies, minimize unplanned downtime, and optimize spare parts inventory levels. In addition, AI-powered predictive modeling enables scenario analysis and what-if simulations, giving decision-makers the ability to evaluate different strategies and effectively mitigate risks.
Wrapping up: Digital transformation for manufacturers in the age of AI

From tracking vast inventories across multiple locations to ensuring that obsolescence notifications are not overlooked, spare parts management has long been a significant challenge for organizations. The sheer volume and complexity of this task has made it nearly impossible for humans, or even dedicated teams, to manage effectively. This has often resulted in accepted inefficiencies and unplanned costs.

However, with the advent of AI and machine learning (ML), a clear solution is now at hand. These technologies are transforming what was once an insurmountable problem into a streamlined, efficient process by enabling the digitization and intelligent management of spare parts.
Innovative tools such as Sparrow are able to analyze, understand, and correct internal spare parts data, easing the burden of managing large inventories. Through the use of AI,
companies can prevent unplanned downtime, avoid missing critical parts, and simplify procurement processes, ultimately leading to significant operational improvements.
Check out our second article in this series, which details how
AI can be used to help you
manage your spare parts
by optimizing your inventory, decision-making, and demand forecasting.

title: Transferwise founder invests in the upcoming Insurtech company Feather (1)

segments.text: Transferwise-Gründer investiert in das Insurtech-Start-up Feather
Feather erhält Investmentrunde in Höhe von €3.8m

Berlin, Deutschland, 5. April 2022 -Transferwise Gründer Taavet Hinrikus hat zusammen mit Sten Tamkivi und anderen Business Angels 3,8 Millionen Euro in Feather investiert, ein deutsches Insurtech-Unternehmen, das bereits mehr als 30.000 Kunden aus über 150 Ländern mit Versicherungen versorgt hat.

Das Unternehmen wurde 2018 von CEO Rob Schumacher, einem ehemaligen McKinsey-Berater, der für einige der größten Versicherungsunternehmen in Europa gearbeitet hat, und CTO Vincent Audoire, einem der ersten Software-Ingenieure des Teams, das N26, eine der größten digitalen Banken in Europa, mit aufgebaut hat, gegründet.

Was Feather von anderen Insurtech-Wettbewerbern unterscheidet, ist die Tatsache, dass das Unternehmen bereits vor der Finanzierungsrunde profitabel war. In der Anfangsphase des Unternehmens war die Versicherungsbranche zu wettbewerbsintensiv, als dass Investoren einen Neueinsteiger in Betracht gezogen hätten. Doch nach der Einführung von neun Versicherungsprodukten in den letzten vier Jahren und der Zusammenarbeit mit einigen der ältesten und bekanntesten Versicherungsunternehmen in Deutschland ist das Unternehmen bereits innovativer als Unternehmen mit größeren Finanzierungsrunden. Als Gründer und CEO eines B2C-Fintech-Unternehmens bringt Taavet nicht nur finanziellen Rückhalt, sondern auch umfassende Erfahrung auf dem Expatriate-Markt mit.

Rob Schumacher: “Durch Bootstrapping haben wir ein wirklich solides Unternehmen aufgebaut und waren nicht wirklich auf der Suche nach einer Finanzierung. Uns gefiel, dass wir gezwungen waren, Produkte zu entwickeln, die unsere Kunden zu schätzen wussten - und das schnell. Taavet und Sten waren sofort von unserer Vision begeistert, und schon bei unserem ersten Treffen hatten wir tolle Ideen, wie wir das Geschäft gemeinsam ausbauen können. Wir freuen uns, dass wir ihre funktionale Expertise im Bereich B2C-Fintech und ihre Erfahrung im Aufbau von Unternehmen an Bord haben.

Taavet Hinrikus sagte: “Ich war wirklich beeindruckt, wie weit das Team ohne Finanzierung gekommen ist, und ich bin begeistert, dass eine weitere Branche transparent und digital gemacht wird. Es gibt viele Parallelen zu Transferwise und das Potenzial ist da, ein noch größeres Unternehmen aufzubauen.”

Über Feather: Feather wurde 2018 von Rob Schumacher und Vincent Audoire gegründet, nachdem beide Schwierigkeiten hatten, sich im deutschen Versicherungssystem zurechtzufinden. Sie wollten Versicherungsprodukte entwickeln, die so einfach wie möglich sind. Deshalb entwickelt Feather digitale Versicherungsprozesse, die alle Interaktionen transparent

machen: vom Abschluss über die Schadensmeldung bis hin zur Kündigung. Ziel ist es, den Menschen eine ehrliche und unvoreingenommene Beratung mit den Informationen zu bieten, die sie brauchen, um die richtige Entscheidung für ihr Leben zu treffen.
Feather raises €3.8m from several unicorn founders

Berlin, Germany, 5th of April 2022.Transferwise founder Taavet Hinrikus has invested €3.8m in Feather, alongside founders or C-level executives from Monzo, N26, GoCardless and insurance experts involved in building Clark and Element. Feather is an insurtech company in Germany that has so far helped more than 30,000 customers from more than 150 countries with their insurance.

The company was founded in 2018 by Rob Schumacher, a former McKinsey consultant with a PhD in actuarial science (insurance mathematics), and Vincent Audoire, one of the first software engineers at N26, one of the largest digital banking companies in Europe.

Feather stood out because they were already profitable and had not raised a seed round, despite having a team of 20. After meeting at Entrepreneur First, Rob and Vincent took this unusual route because they thought "money wouldn't help them go any faster", and launching nine insurance products over the last four years has proved them right.

Rob Schumacher said: "By bootstrapping we built a really healthy business and were not actually looking for funding. We liked that we were forced to build products that customers would value - quickly. Taavet and Sten were immediately excited by our vision and in our very first meeting we came up with some great ideas to grow the business together. We are excited to have their functional expertise in B2C Fintech, but also their experience in building companies on board".

Taavet Hinrikus said: "I was really impressed by how far the team has come without funding, and I am excited to see another industry become transparent and digital. There are many parallels with Wise, and the potential is there to build an even bigger company".

About Feather: Feather was founded in 2018 by Rob Schumacher and Vincent Audoire, after both struggled to navigate the insurance system in Germany. That's why Feather builds insurance to make all interactions easier and more transparent: from signing up, to filing a claim, to cancelling. The aim is to give honest, unbiased advice, with all the information you need to make the right decision. And because insurance is so complicated, Feather provides tools, articles and support where people can talk to a human about problems or questions they have.
Currently, Feather has helped people from over 150 countries buy insurance digitally and is expanding rapidly.

title: Wie profitieren KUKA-Roboter von KI?

segments.text: Automatisierungstechnologien haben die industrielle Produktion revolutioniert, doch ihr Potenzial bleibt in vielen Branchen ungenutzt. Genau hier setzt die Partnerschaft zwischen Micropsi Industries und KUKA an: Durch die Kombination der innovativen KI-Vision von Micropsi Industries mit den robusten Robotern von KUKA können nun auch Anwendungen in neuen Märkten und Branchen automatisiert werden, die bisher als zu komplex galten. Zu Industries‘ MIRAI erfolgreich meistert, gehören End-of-Line-den Anwendungen, die Micropsi Tests, Montage, Leckageprüfung und Gestellbestückung.
Von Micropsi Industries

Bei Micropsi Industries erleben wir täglich, welches Potenzial in – ein Potenzial, das weit über die Automatisierungstechnologien steckt Automobilindustrie, unsere Kernkompetenz, hinausgeht und in vielen anderen Branchen noch ungenutzt ist. Viele der Technologien, die in der Automobilindustrie entwickelt und eingesetzt werden, haben andere Produktionsbereiche noch nicht erreicht. Für diese Branchen ergibt sich jedoch die Möglichkeit, auf bereits erprobte Lösungen der Automobilindustrie zurückzugreifen und sie in ihre eigenen Prozesse zu integrieren. Dieses Potenzial ist jedoch vielen noch nicht bewusst.

Kürzlich sprachen wir mit einem Kunden, der eine große Anzahl von Servern betreibt. Diese Server enthalten mehrere Komponenten, die regelmäßig – ausgetauscht werden, bevor sie ausfallen, um technische Störungen zu vermeiden ein Standard in der Branche. Der Kunde berichtete uns, dass er einen Roboter in Form eines Oktopusses entwickelt, um diesen Prozess zu automatisieren, ohne zu wissen, dass Roboterarme in der Automobilindustrie bereits ähnliche Aufgaben übernehmen.

Derzeit besteht eine Kluft zwischen dem, was die Technik tatsächlich leisten kann, und dem, was viele für möglich halten. Fachleute in spezialisierten Bereichen wie der Serverwartung wissen oft nicht, dass Technologien, wie sie in der Automobilindustrie eingesetzt werden, auf ihre eigenen Anwendungen übertragbar sind - inklusive der erforderlichen Präzision und Zuverlässigkeit.

Betrachten wir einige häufige Anwendungen in Montage- und Fertigungsprozessen, wie zum Beispiel das Bestücken von Gestellen, das Verschrauben oder die Leckageprüfung. Diese Aufgaben sind oft schwer zu automatisieren, da sie mit einem Phänomen konfrontiert sind, das als Varianz bezeichnet wird. Varianz tritt häufig in fünf Formen auf: Position, Form, Licht, Farbe und Hintergrund. Um dieses Problem zu lösen, werden Industrieroboter mit Vision-Systemen ausgestattet, die es ihnen ermöglichen, Varianzen zu erkennen und entsprechend zu reagieren.
Herkömmliche Vision-Systeme sind oft aufwendig einzurichten, benötigen komple
xe
CAD-Daten

und müssen bei neuen Varianzen häufig umprogrammiert werden. Viele Unternehmen in der Fertigungsindustrie versuchen daher, dieses Problem auf die übliche Weise zu lösen, indem sie neue Mitarbeiter einstellen, die diese Aufgaben manuell erledigen können.

Das Problem, mit dem sich die Hersteller jedoch zunehmend konfrontiert sehen, ist der Mangel an qualifizierten Arbeitskräften für diese Stellen. Die Unternehmen sind daher gezwungen, die Automatisierung als die einzige Lösung in Betracht zu ziehen. Auch der Jahresbericht de
r International Federation of Robotics (IFR)
zeigt diesen klaren Trend: Die Zahl der Industrieroboter in der automatisierten Produktion steigt in vielen Ländern kontinuierlich an.

Südkorea steht mit 1 000 installierten Industrierobotern pro 10 000 Beschäftigten weltweit an der Spitze. Es folgen Singapur (670), Japan (399) und Deutschland (397). Obwohl diese Zahlen seit der Pandemie kontinuierlich steigen, ist es noch ein weiter Weg, bis die Fabriken die Automatisierung verlässlich ausweiten können, um den Fachkräftemangel auszugleichen.
Das technologische Plateau

Industrieroboter sind aus der Produktion nicht mehr wegzudenken. Seit Jahrzehnten werden sie zuverlässig produziert und eingesetzt. Diejenigen, die schon länger in der Industrie tätig sind, haben wahrscheinlich alle Jahre wieder die Prognosen gehört, Roboter die Produktion vollständig übernehmen und sogenannte „dunkle dass Fabriken“ ohne menschliche Arbeitskräfte entstehen werden. Seit Anfang der 2000er-Jahre werden diese Vorhersagen wiederholt, ohne dass nennenswerte Fortschritte erzielt wurden.

Ein Grund dafür ist, dass unsere wirtschaftspolitische Situation weltweit und auch die Lieferketten bis vor Kurzem relativ stabil waren. Seit dem Ausbruch der Coronapandemie haben wir jedoch eine Reihe internationaler Krisen erlebt, die die – mit direkten Auswirkungen auf die globalen Lieferketten erheblich gestört haben Art und Weise, wie die Produktion bisher funktioniert hat. Hinzu kommt der Fachkräftemangel, der die Hersteller dazu zwingt, auf neue Technologien zu setzen, um flexibler zu werden.

Was die Hardware angeht, haben wir im Wesentlichen ein technologisches Plateau erreicht. Die Roboter, die in den letzten Jahrzehnten produziert wurden, unterscheiden sich nicht wesentlich von denen, die heute hergestellt werden. So ist es nicht ungewöhnlich, einen 25 Jahre alten KUKA-Roboter zu sehen, der seit dem Jahr 2000 treu dieselbe Aufgabe erfüllt.
Gleichzeitig hat die Zahl der Industrieroboter, die unterschiedliche Aufgaben übernehmen können, in den letzten Jahren stark zugenommen. Neue
Softwareentwicklungen haben dazu beigetragen, die Einsatzmöglichkeiten dieser Roboter erheblich zu erweitern.
Die Partnerschaft zwischen Micropsi Industries und KUKA

Micropsi Industries wurde in Deutschland gegründet mit einer Kernkompetenz in der Automobilindustrie, in der auch KUKA am stärksten vertreten ist. In unseren ersten Jahren besuchten wir häufig Fabriken in Deutschland, sprachen mit den Menschen auf dem Shopfloor und sahen KUKA-Roboter in fast jeder Produktionslinie. KUKA wurde für uns zu einem Symbol des Erfolgs und wir erkannten schon damals, dass eine Partnerschaft und die Integration unserer Software in KUKA-Robotern für beide Unternehmen einen großen Vorteil am Markt bringen würde.

In den ersten Gesprächen konnten wir deutlich machen, dass unsere Software MIRAI nicht nur zuverlässig funktioniert, sondern mit ihrer visionbasierten Steuerung für Roboter auch einzigartig ist. Daraufhin wurden wir zu unserem ersten Partner- Event mit KUKA eingeladen und unser Team richtete innerhalb weniger Stunden – nahezu einzigartig in der eine MIRAI-Demonstration auf einer neuen Maschine ein Branche. – so Mittlerweile präsentieren wir KUKA-Roboter mit MIRAI regelmäßig auf Messen auch 2023 bei unserem ersten Showcase auf der Automatica in München.
Was MIRAI für KUKA-Roboter ermöglicht
Obwohl KUKA zu den weltweit führenden Anbietern von Industrierobotern zählt, kann kein Unternehmen alle Automatisierungsaufgaben allein lösen. Deshalb ist KUKA auf starke Partnerschaften angewiesen.

Die Partnerschaft zwischen Micropsi Industries und KUKA bringt beiden Unternehmen und ihren Kunden zahlreiche Vorteile. Für KUKA bedeutet sie, dass ihre Roboter nun in der Lage sind, Aufgaben zu automatisieren, die ein KI- gesteuertes Vision-System erfordern. Dadurch können Kunden ihre Industrieroboter für komplexere Aufgaben einsetzen und KUKA kann mehr Roboter für solche Anwendungen verkaufen.
Durch die Kombination von KUKA-Robotern und MIRAI von Micropsi Industries lassen sich folgende Aufgaben automatisieren:
1. End-of-Line-Tests 2. Montage 3. Gestellbestückung 4. Verschrauben 5. Picking 6. Leckageprüfung

Für diejenigen, die mit traditionellen Vision-Systemen vertraut sind, mögen diese Anwendungen anspruchsvoll erscheinen. Was MIRAI jedoch im Vergleich zu Vision- Systemen einzigartig macht, ist die Fähigkeit, Aufgaben zu bewältigen, die mit anderen Systemen nicht möglich sind. MIRAI-gesteuerte Roboter können zuverlässig mit reflektierenden und transparenten Objekten umgehen. Im Gegensatz zu herkömmlichen Methoden benötigt MIRAI weder detaillierte 3-D-Modelle noch zeitaufwendige Kamerakalibrierungen, sondern lernt durch Demonstrationen und reagiert in Echtzeit auf Abweichungen.

Darüber hinaus kann MIRAI innerhalb weniger Tage statt Wochen oder Monate implementiert werden und dank seiner Flexibilität können Konfigurationen ebenso schnell an Prozessänderungen angepasst werden. Wir stellen unseren Kunden außerdem ein spezialisiertes Customer-Success-Team zur Verfügung, das rund um die Uhr Unterstützung bei Implementierung, Skalierung und Wartung einer zuverlässigen Automatisierungslösung bietet.
KUKA und Micropsi Industries setzen damit einen neuen Standard in der Automation. Weitere Informationen zu MIRAI finden Si
e auf unserer Website.
Englische Version --
How KUKA robots benefit from AI

Automation technologies have revolutionized industrial production, but their potential remains untapped in many industries. By combining Micropsi Industries' AI vision software with KUKA's robust robots, it is now possible to automate applications in new markets and industries that were previously considered too complex.
From Micropsi Industries

— potential that At Micropsi Industries, we see firsthand the vast potential of automation technologies extends far beyond our core automotive expertise and remains untapped in many other industries. While the automotive industry has been instrumental in driving and refining many new technologies, these advancements have yet to find their way into other areas of manufacturing. This presents an exciting opportunity for other industries to adopt tested and proven solutions and integrate them into their own processes. However, this opportunity often goes unnoticed.

For example, we recently spoke with a customer who manages a large server infrastructure. These servers — a standard industry practice. contain multiple components that are routinely replaced to prevent failure The customer explained how they were developing an octopus-shaped robot to automate this process, unaware that robotic arms in the automotive industry already perform similar tasks efficiently.

This highlights a critical knowledge gap: what technology can do today versus what many believe it can do. Specialists in fields such as server maintenance are often unaware that technologies designed for the automotive sector can meet their needs with the same level of precision and reliability.
Consider common manufacturing and assembly tasks such as rack hanging, screwdriving, or leak detection. These are often difficult to automate due to a challenge known as variance, which generally

comes in five forms when looking at it from a manufacturing perspective: position, shape, light, color, and background. To overcome this, industrial robots are equipped with vision software/systems that enable them to detect and adapt to this variance.
However, traditional vision systems present significant challenges. They are complex to set up, often require detailed
CAD data,
and require frequent reprogramming to accommodate new variations. As a result, many companies rely on manual labor to perform these tasks instead.
Yet manufacturers are increasingly constrained by a shortage of skilled workers to fill these roles. This has made automation not just an option but a necessity. The annual report of the
International Federation of
Robotics (IFR)
confirms this trend: The use of industrial robots in automated production continues to grow worldwide.
South Korea currently leads the world with
1,000 industrial robots installed per 10,000 workers,

followed by Singapore (670), Japan (399) and Germany (397). While these numbers have steadily increased since the pandemic, there is still a long way to go before factories can reliably scale automation to address labor shortages.
The technological plateau

Industrial robots have become an essential part of the manufacturing process. They have been reliably built and used for decades. Those who have been in the industry long enough have heard the repeated predictions that robots will completely take over production, leading to so-called "dark factories" without human workers. These predictions have been made since the early 2000s without significant progress.

One reason is that the global economic and political landscape, as well as supply chains, have been relatively stable until recently. However, since the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic, we have experienced a series of international crises that have significantly disrupted global supply chains - directly impacting traditional manufacturing operations. In addition, there is a shortage of skilled labor, forcing manufacturers to adopt new technologies to become more agile.

In terms of hardware, we have also essentially reached a technological plateau. The robots produced over the past few decades are not significantly different from those produced today. It is, therefore, not uncommon to see a 25-year-old KUKA robot still reliably performing the same task it was assigned in 2000.

At the same time, the number of industrial robots capable of performing a wide variety of tasks has increased significantly in recent years. Thanks to new software developments, the range of applications for these robots has been greatly expanded.
The partnership between Micropsi Industries and KUKA

Micropsi Industries was founded in Germany with a core competency in the automotive industry, which is also where KUKA has a strong presence. In our early years, we frequently visited factories in Germany, talked to people on the shop floor, and saw KUKA robots on almost every production line. For us, KUKA became a symbol of success, and we realized early on that a partnership and integration of our software with KUKA robots would create a significant market advantage for both companies.

In our initial discussions, we were able to demonstrate that our software, MIRAI, was not only reliable but also unique in its vision-based control of robots. Impressed with our product, KUKA then invited us to our first partner event, where our team set up a MIRAI demonstration on a new machine in just a few hours, an almost unheard-of occurrence in the industry for this type of technology.
Today, we regularly showcase KUKA robots with MIRAI at trade shows, including our first showcase at Automatica in Munich in 2023.
The benefits of MIRAI for KUKA Robots
Although KUKA is one of the world's leading suppliers of industrial robots, no company can solve all automation tasks on its own. That is why KUKA relies on strong partnerships.

The partnership between Micropsi Industries and KUKA offers many benefits to both companies and their customers. For KUKA, it means that its robots can now automate tasks that require an AI-driven vision system. This allows customers to use their industrial robots for more complex tasks and allows KUKA to sell more robots for such applications.
Currently, the combination of KUKA robots and Micropsi Industries’ MIRAI is being used to automate:
1. End-of-line testing 2. Insertion 3. Rack hanging 4. Screwdriving 5. Picking 6. Leak detection

For those familiar with traditional vision systems, these applications may seem challenging. However, what makes MIRAI unique compared to other vision systems is its ability to handle tasks that are impossible with other systems. MIRAI-guided robots can reliably work with reflective and transparent objects. Unlike conventional methods, MIRAI does not require detailed 3D models or time-consuming camera calibrations. Instead, it learns through demonstrations and responds to deviations in real-time.

In addition, MIRAI can be implemented in days rather than weeks or months. Its flexibility allows configurations to be quickly adapted to process changes. We also provide our customers with a dedicated Customer Success Team that provides around-the-clock support for implementing, scaling, and maintaining a reliable automation solution.
Together, KUKA and Micropsi Industries are setting a new standard in automation. For more information on MIRAI,
please visit our website.
